I find myself busy long after others are asleep. I'm ready to start again early in the A.M. The truth is I can't get enough of life. Some have called it "the fire from within." In mythology it's known as "opening the third eye." For me it's been the energy to stay the course, to persevere, to be the last man standing.

They argue that trepanning increases the volume of blood that can get to the brain. Analogizing it to the fontanelle (the “soft spot” that all babies have in their skull at birth), they conclude that it restores childlike health, creativity, and ability to grow. They join mainstream medicine in recommending against self-trepanation, but seem to have found an anonymous Mexican surgeon who would do it for only $2,400. No wonder they got so many volunteers:

As late as 2018, the ITAG website (trepan.com) said they were busy trying to do pilot studies to verify their claims. But in 2019, the site went down, and I can’t find any evidence that the organization continues to exist. After over 10,000 years, it seems like this ancient practice is well and truly gone.

item.title: San Francisco Meetup This Saturday
item.content:encoded:
Why: We’re having our usual round of fall meetups, and San Francisco is one of them. I’m signal-boosting this one because it’s likely to be our biggest, and because I plan to be there. I’ll do a Q&A if the sound system is up for it.

When: Saturday, October 24, 1 PM to late afternoon

Where: Mox, 1680 Mission St, San Francisco, CA 94103. Please RSVP here for the door code, we will work to make sure people without the code still get in but it’ll be quicker and more reliable if as many people as possible have it.

Who: Anyone who wants. You don’t have to pay money or know anything about the blog. Please feel free to come even if you feel awkward about it, even if you’re not “the typical ACX reader”, even if you’re worried people won’t like you, etc. You’re unlikely to be an outlier, regardless of whether you’re very weird, very normie, or somewhere in between.

Anyone who is caught expressing policy opinions will be herded into a side room and made to help create a San Francisco voting guide; if you expect this to be you, consider bringing your laptop or ballot materials.

item.title: Your Book Review: The Ghost In My Brain
item.description: Finalist #13 in the Book Review Contest
item.content:encoded:
[This is one of the finalists in the 2026 book review contest, written by an ACX reader who will remain anonymous until after voting is done. I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked]

In 1999, Professor Clark Elliott is rear-ended by a stranger at a stoplight. He’s shaken but figures he’s fine, and drives to work. Spoiler: Clark Elliott is not fine.

Elliott is severely concussed, and this fact will dictate the next ten years of his life. Elliott’s memoir is based on notes he took while concussed. Reading it is like watching someone try to troubleshoot their broken laptop using the broken laptop.

In the opening chapter, Elliott describes walking from his office to his car after a long winter workday:

“At this point my world had collapsed inward on itself… I looked down at my feet and shouted at myself to walk, but I knew it was hopeless. I had lost the mysterious initiative that impels us all forward when we walk, and I knew that without brain rest I wouldn’t be getting it back. I considered lying down in the snow.”

Over an hour later, Elliott finally manages to cross the parking lot and begins the second phase of his trial: getting into the car.

“I’d lost the concept of center. I had no internal representation, or visual understanding of circle, target, middle, inside. Without these concepts I couldn’t get my hand to move toward the lock, or put the key in the slot.” So he just stands next to the door for another hour and a half.

Around 2 a.m., a suspicious police officer asks why Elliott is loitering in the parking lot, but the officer is too cold to get out of his car and drives away. At 3:30 a.m., four and a half hours after he left his office, Elliott finally arrives home.

Somehow, Elliott lives like this for a decade.

The book’s first mystery is how a person can remain conscious, verbal, employed, and yet so damaged that he can’t get into a car or recognize his own house. The second mystery is: why did he apparently recover through treatments that sound, at first pass, like boutique neuro-quackery?

A disclosure is in order before we continue. I am pretty personally invested in the answers here. About a year and a half ago, I got seriously concussed. Milder than Elliott’s, but bad enough to substantially rearrange my life. On some level, I read this book in hope of a cheap fix, or at least an obvious one. Instead I found myself in the weird borderlands of modern medicine.

A hurricane let loose on 50 million desktop computers

What’s it like to be a human with severe brain damage? Elliott offers a metaphor:

To simulate concussion damage to a human brain then, we’ll need to gather together […] 50 million desktop computers, a 500,000-mile-high stack of paper, and the almost inconceivable amount of information it takes to construct a human mind, then loose a hurricane on the system, ripping out network lines, laying waste to vast sections of memory, and sending landslides to smash hundreds of thousands of computers.

A bit sensational, but you get the picture. One classic model of what’s happening during severe concussions is “diffuse axonal injury”: rapid acceleration and deceleration stretch axons, the neuron projections that send electrical signals, causing micro-tears and disrupting cellular metabolism.

Standard CT and MRI imaging usually fail to detect these microscopic or functional disruptions, and there isn’t really a cure, so patients are told to go home, rest up, and wait to find out whether they’ll be back to work the next day or out of commission for the next decade.

U.S. concussion incidence is commonly cited around 1.6-3.8 million a year, and many go unreported1 . About 15-30% of adults report post-concussion symptoms (PCS) 3-6 months later. Even on conservative estimates, that’s hundreds of thousands of cases a year in the US alone. A much smaller number of those cases will result in something like Elliott’s experience.

After the initial fender-bender, Elliott hands his driver’s license to the other driver. Then, a few minutes later, he hands it over again. He has no memory of having done so the first time, and can’t figure out why people are looking at him funny. This is a recurring theme—Elliott can’t even notice the problem, because the cognition that’s supposed to monitor the behavior has gone offline.

He writes: “when cognitive capabilities go missing they are often so fully gone that the concussive does not miss them in the way a normal person would, or indeed sometimes even realize they’ve gone absent.”

But Clark Elliott is no pushover. He’s a Professor of Artificial Intelligence at DePaul University, a consummate musician, is single-handedly renovating his family home, and runs marathons on the side. The biographical lists serve a purpose: Elliott wants to assure the reader that he hasn’t become less intelligent. His cognitive capacities have just come apart in a way that doesn’t track any nameable cognitive disorder.

He can write, but he cannot read. He can climb stairs but not descend them. He can teach a graduate seminar and then, walking home afterward, fail to recognize his own house. Moving through doorways or down halls poses a significant challenge.

More than once, he describes his state as “alien.” He writes, “we still walk and talk and act as though we are part of the human race, but it doesn’t feel that way inside… Instead, there is a strange feeling of nostalgia, a longing for who we used to be.” He notes that this feeling of disconnection is likely a significant contributor to the rate of suicide among concussives2 : “we have, in many ways, already lost that which makes us human.”

One of the most striking passages in the book is when Elliott, hungry, decides to make himself a snack. He heads to the kitchen to eat a piece of salami and an apple, but finds he can’t. As though trapped in an old Tom and Jerry cartoon, he finds himself literally unable to choose which of the two to eat first. He can’t initiate action selection. He goes to the living room, returns to the kitchen, fails again. He repeats this loop ten times, like “a rat repeatedly traversing a dead-end maze.” Two days pass before he eats.

Elliott calls this “getting stuck.” The bridge between knowing what he wants to do and doing it has broken. In desperation, he finally calls his bemused friend Jake, who tells him: “Okay, go eat the salami first, then eat the apple,” ending the forty-eight hours of struggle.

Somehow, he cobbles together enough coping mechanisms to keep limping along for years. Until he can’t anymore.

Partial death

“This is it,” Elliott reflected. “I am never going to have another normal day, or hour, or ten-minute period again. I am never going to be a real human being again. I won’t be publishing my research, and at some point I am going to lose my job.”

Ten years after the crash, Elliott is approaching a complete breakdown. Or rather, while broken, he adds a small child to the equation. As it turns out, the normal prattle of his two-year-old daughter is concussion kryptonite:

“It was this simple combination—my inability to filter out or process spoken dialogue in real time, and Erin’s continual need to talk—that almost led to a final, catastrophic meltdown.” He calls it “partial death.”

Unfortunately, there are no parenting sabbaticals. In a last-ditch effort, Elliott pulls out his emergency savings and reaches out to a “cognitive restructuring specialist” named Donalee Markus.

Wait a minute, you might be thinking. Elliott hasn’t seen a specialist before??

He has, sort of. It didn’t help. A brief detour through medical history: Elliott hit his head in 1999. The CDC didn’t publish its first major report on mild traumatic brain injury (TBI) until 2003. The NFL concussion crisis broke into public awareness in 2005. Until 2013, the only mention of persistent post-concussive symptoms in the DSM-IV was in the appendix under “proposed criteria set”. After the crash, an ER doctor checks his pupils and sends him home; a neurologist runs a 30-minute test and declares him fine, and shouts at him when he pushes back.

It’s unclear whether Elliott was just unlucky in encountering a cast of extremely unsympathetic medical professionals, or whether this was really the general state of neurology in the 90s. Whatever the case, Elliott quickly writes the whole system off and goes back to calling his friend Jake whenever he gets stuck in doorways.

The Miracle Begins

For ten years, Elliott can’t make himself a sandwich. Then, over the course of a year, he substantially recovers. Enter idiosyncratic concussion specialists Donalee Markus and Deborah Zelinsky.

This is the first time we have a third-person perspective on Elliott. Markus writes:

“Clark Elliott was a mystery to me when we first met. Observing him through my glass front door, I saw that it took him two minutes just to find the doorknob with his hand. When I gave him the simplest of my assessment tests—copying a geometric line drawing—his body went into bizarre contortions as he struggled to complete it.” Markus takes him on as a patient anyway.

Her intervention is simple: she gives him geometric puzzles to solve, specifically trapezoids and three-dimensional dot exercises that escalate in complexity. He has to apply rules to shapes, generate equations from them, and eventually do the whole thing in his head.

(Source): Elliot includes a bunch of these geometric puzzle examples in the book. Sadly, they didn’t alleviate my symptoms.

Markus also refers Elliott to her colleague Deborah Zelinsky, a neuro-optometrist.

Bells and Prisms

Zelinsky’s diagnostic method is a little more involved. The patient closes their eyes, and the examiner rings a small bell at various positions in space. The patient must reach out to touch the bell. The patient will often fail this test, revealing a “visual-auditory mismatch.” Zelinsky will then try different prism lens combinations while the patient’s eyes are closed and ask them to do the bell test again. I repeat, the patient’s eyes remain fully closed. The entire time. She then prescribes the lenses that improve the patient’s performance.

This is called the Z-bell test (presumably after “Zelinsky,” who has a patent on it). While I wasn’t particularly surprised that adjusting someone’s vision when their eyes are open can change how accurately they localize sound when their eyes are closed, I remain deeply confused about how prism lenses could alter accuracy if the patient’s eyes remain closed the entire time.

The claim is that low-level light still passes through the closed eyelids, stimulates retinal activity, and that this stimulation is what’s being modulated by the different lenses.

Zelinsky’s Mind-Eye Institute website:

“By placing various types of lenses across a patient’s closed eyes, we can change the way light spreads over the retina, thus modifying the dynamic relationship between the mind’s visual inputs and the body’s internal responses.”

Depending on wavelength, eyelids transmit somewhere from well under 1% of blue/green light to around 5–6% of red light. But, as anyone with eyelids knows, this is still mostly diffuse reddish illumination—not sufficient to update your visual field, or to localize a bell.

But within a year of meeting Markus and Zelinsky, Elliott has experienced massive improvements and is on the road to recovery. He writes a heartfelt note to Markus thanking her for “giving him his life back.” So I guess the treatments worked?

Into the uncanny valley of concussion science

Let’s take a look at the evidence, starting with Markus. Markus belongs to a fairly large tradition of “cognitive training interventions” for PCS for which there’s some evidence. A 2016 meta-analysis looking at 14 studies on cognitive training in post-acute TBI found a small effect on overall improvement in cognitive function (Hallock et al., 2016).

Unfortunately, “cognitive rehabilitation” is an enormous umbrella and Markus’s specific protocol isn’t in the meta-analysis. Markus published her own protocol in 2007, describing the puzzle-based technique she used on Elliott, but it’s more of a “how I do it” piece, not a controlled trial. The trail of scientific evidence dries up there.

Okay, what about Zelinsky? Do the bells work? There’s a 2019 paper that tried to find out. First author: Clark Elliott.

The paper is a preliminary conference paper on 14 out of the 41 recruited participants. Elliott et al. find that the therapeutic lenses produced a small but statistically significant improvement in bell-touching accuracy compared to the clear-lens baseline. However, the therapeutic lenses didn’t outperform an ‘impaired lens’ condition, which was theorized to push the outcome in the opposite direction, and the full study with all 41 recruited participants has never been published.

This is pretty tepid evidence. With one preliminary, ambiguous analysis its only empirical bulwark against the wave of scientific skepticism, Zelinsky’s method isn’t looking too good.

That said, the testimonial evidence is abundant. “I can move normally again, be active, travel. Mind-Eye has opened up a whole new chapter in my life,” says an avid patient. One testimonial describes the treatment as “like, well, ‘magic,’” while another patient calls it “mathemagical.”

We can add Clark Elliott to the rave reviewers. Within ten days of his first prism glasses, he reports a strange shift. Music sounds different, and he starts re-accessing visual scenes from childhood.

Within a month, Elliott begins to feel like himself again. The “ghost of his true self” had reentered the room. “At last I had enough brain power to support the real me, the complex me. I could see the world through my own eyes again.”

The strongest within-book evidence that the glasses, in particular, are doing causal work comes from what happens when Elliott briefly loses them. Even 33 hours without his prescription produces dramatic regression: exhaustion, handwriting deterioration, visual disturbances, and the return of the “all tasks involve pain in some way” baseline of his pre-recovery life. Once he finds the glasses, he’s back to playing the Beatles from memory and “looking forward to the rest of [his life] again.”

Elliott is writing the book fifteen years after the accident, and the recovery has held. He even claims, with the partial qualification one expects from a man who has nearly lost his mind to a brain injury, that his cognition is in some ways now better than it was before the crash.

A skeptical explanation might be that Elliott was desperate and ripe for placebo effect. Receiving intense attention from clinicians who believed they could help him after years of failed encounters with doctors might have been sufficient to shift his symptoms. Elliott’s recovery was staged over five years with iterative adjustments, which is exactly the protocol that would maintain a placebo effect, and the base rate of spontaneous recovery in chronic PCS is non-zero. So can we be sure that any of these treatments did anything other than give him a pat on the back as the concussion worked itself out?

I think a case can be made for at least some real intervention. While the evidence for Zelinsky’s closed-eye method in particular is thin, the general “prescribe new lenses” approach looks much more promising. There’s even a reasonable causal mechanism on offer.

If you hold up your thumb in front of your face, and then easily switch between looking at something on the wall and your thumb, congrats - your accommodation triad is working. The accommodation triad is the trio of ocular functions that enable close-up vision. In many PCS patients, this system goes awry, resulting in a suite of vision complications. In a study of adolescent patients (n=116), Wiecek et al (2021) found that ~60% of patients had deficits in near point of convergence after concussion. Prism lenses can reduce eye strain by shifting the image on the retina so the eyes don’t have to work as hard to converge, and magnifying lenses reduce accommodation demand.

A year into my concussion, and partially inspired by Elliott, I asked my neuro-opthalmologist for prism lenses. They didn’t help at all. But the magnifying lenses I tried next totally did, almost entirely eliminating my symptoms immediately (unfortunately, they later returned).

It’s possible that Zelinsky’s method actually does work, but not for the reason she thinks. The bell ceremony might just be an unusually elaborate way to arrive at a genuinely useful prescription.

This would explain both her rave reviews and the lack of scientific support. Her Z-bell tinkering isn’t doing much, but the broader lens intervention sometimes works—some percent of the time, prism glasses and magnifying lenses actually do improve people’s concussion symptoms. (Of course, this will result in a hit-or-miss treatment, but you can’t tell because none of the duds post a review).

When averages fail

So what, if anything, can we learn from Elliott’s recovery?

Here’s one obvious point: recovery is possible, but strangely elusive. It took Elliott a decade, several awful medical encounters, and two boutique specialists to find help. While the situation was worse in the 90s, it’s still bad today. In one study, among patients severe enough to reach specialty care, fewer than a third had recovered when surveyed, and the still-symptomatic group had been living with PCS for an average of 4.5 years (Hiploylee et al., 2017).

Perhaps the real mystery is: why is it so hard to treat concussions?

One reason is that concussions resist mainstream medical intervention. Clinical instruments can’t catch the microscopic damage common to PCS, and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) struggle to identify treatments when the population is heterogeneous and the symptoms are varied and subjective. So it takes months to get a PCS diagnosis, and even when you do, many clinicians have no idea what to do with you.

PCS treatment is hard because concussion does not damage an abstract, average brain. It damages your brain, with your particular foibles and weak spots. Specialist concussion medicine has identified roughly six clinical phenotypes, but even when correctly type-cast, each patient responds differently. Clark Elliott and I both had vision issues, but he responded to prisms while magnifying lenses worked for me. PCS may be less like a single disease than a family resemblance category with wildly different failures compressed into one diagnosis.

RCTs are the “medical gold standard.” But perhaps idiosyncratic medical maladies are where the standard hierarchy of evidence breaks down a little. Philosopher of science Nancy Cartwright has argued that RCTs answer a narrower question than clinical practice needs: they tell you that a treatment, on average, produced a particular outcome in a trial population. They don’t tell you whether it will work for you in particular.

So PCS patients navigate the uncanny valley of niche medical science: on the one side, RCTs and rigorous studies that document average effects that might not apply to you, and on the other, N=1 case studies that might solve your exact problem, or be entirely useless. In the middle, there’s a bunch of people trying to sell you metabolism-enhancing lasers for five thousand dollars. Absent clear explanations, patients can find themselves passed between neurologists, optometrists, physical therapists, vision therapists, acupuncturists, psychiatrists, and energy-healers before finding the one thing that happens to work for them.

To get the most juice out of a clinical trial, you need a theory of why the treatment worked, for whom, and whether you’re similar enough to the trial population for the effect to transfer.

But what if you don’t have a mature theory yet?

Z-bell tests and Fijian reef fish

As a species, we’ve been solving problems we don’t understand for a long time. On Fiji’s Yasawa Island, pregnant and breastfeeding women observe taboos against eating certain species of reef fish. When Natalie and Joseph Henrich investigated in 2010, they found that the taboo species mapped onto the fish most likely to carry ciguatera toxin, a naturally occurring marine toxin that’s particularly dangerous to fetuses and nursing infants. Local variation combined with fitness-relevant outcomes and social learning can surface solutions long before the mechanism is understood. (The trade-off is that sometimes they suggest you try bloodletting or child sacrifice).

For poorly understood chronic conditions, treatment often looks less like applying established science and more like janky cultural learning. PCS communities generate variation, share outcomes online, and copy apparently successful interventions.

But what makes the Fijian case work is that there’s a real selector pulling signal out of the noise. Toxic fish made people visibly sick, and useful taboos could be reinforced across generations. The PCS testimonial ecosystem has no comparably reliable selector; variants can propagate just because they’re dramatic or recent or someone’s trying to sell you something. The same dynamics that make it kind of reasonable to try Zelinsky’s Z-bell test might push you toward forty sessions of hyperbaric oxygen at $200 a pop.

Another drawback is that cultural transmission is good at producing outcomes, but overimitates methods. The Z-bell case is actually a nice illustration. Even if Zelinsky’s lenses actually help some patients, the community’s causal story (closed-eye retinal stimulation) might be totally wrong. Cultural transmission will faithfully convey the bells-and-mathemagic ritual along with whatever genuinely works.

Alright, clearly we can’t just trust the forums. In an ideal world, we’d capitalize on the strengths of patient communities (lots of people trying lots of things) and combine it with some kind of rigorous selection mechanism.

Luckily, there’s already a proof of concept for this. In 2020, the Body Politic COVID support group pioneered a novel idea: ask patients stuff. They created the Patient-Generated Hypotheses Journal (PGHJ) and began advising (and funding) major research efforts. Their flagship peer-reviewed paper (Davis et al, 2021), an online survey of 3,762 people drawn from support groups across 56 countries, found that Long COVID affected multiple organ systems, that symptoms persisted well past acute infection, and that recovery often took many months (all borne out by subsequent research).

Some community-amplified hypotheses won’t hold up—great, that’s what science is for! At the least, the PGHJ demonstrates that heterogenous patient communities can do more than swap miracle stories; they can generate structured observations and funnel hypotheses toward controlled studies. For example, do prism glasses actually improve general cognitive functioning in PCS patients with convergence issues? Despite Elliott’s popularization, as far as I can tell there are literally no RCTs testing this.

For medical orphans like PCS, the evidence hierarchy is doing the right things in the wrong order. Population-wide RCTs belong at the top once we know what outcome we care about and what mechanism we’re targeting. Until then, structured patient case registries could help us figure out what actually deserves a trial.

Getting out of the parking lot

Two years ago, if someone asked me how to navigate PCS, I would have said, “Uh, only pursue treatments with clear, scientifically-backed benefits.”

And at first, that’s what I did. My path to recovery started with best-evidenced treatments. But as the months dragged on without improvement, I found myself in testimonial-land—trying things based on Google Maps reviews, and reading this book.

As a concussion roadmap, The Ghost in My Brain is pretty frustrating. Elliott is too ready to accept his clinicians’ explanations and treats his recovery path as way more generalizable than it is. But as phenomenology, it’s excellent. It does a great job of conveying what it feels like when your brain breaks. If you’re intrigued by the extreme edges of human experience, this is for you. If you’re looking for a guidebook, sorry, there isn’t one (yet).

For conditions like severe, persistent PCS, the patients who recover often fall into two groups: the ones who are lucky enough to find clinicians willing to iterate with them, and the ones who have the time and money to experiment on themselves. That’s a small slice of the population.

We can’t just replace RCTs with facebook groups, but maybe we could bridge the weirdness of individual cases and the discipline of controlled science. The rather dark irony here is that the PCS patient community has PCS. Many of us can’t look at screens, nevermind organize case registries. But if even the conservative end of the PCS estimates is right, that’s hundreds of thousands of cases a year. Many of those people are doing exactly what I did—trawling through forums and trying treatments. And whether or not anyone records the results, people will continue to search the solution space. Because when your brain breaks and you’re stuck in apple vs salami hell, you try all the bells and prisms.

1

Institute of Medicine and National Research Council. Sports-Related Concussions in Youth: Improving the Science, Changing the Culture. National Academies Press, 2014, citing Langlois et al. 2006. This is technically a report on sports and recreation-related TBI and concussion, which are overlapping categories that both often lead to PCS. Given that this is just sports and rec related, the real number must be much higher.

2

A major JAMA Neurology meta-analysis found a relative risk of suicide of 2.03 after concussion/mild TBI. In two included cohort studies with about 4 years median follow-up, suicide deaths occurred in 0.50% and 0.59% of diagnosed concussion/mTBI patients. That is roughly 1 in 200 over that follow-up period

item.title: My California Ballot, 2026
item.content:encoded:
See also ACX meetup groups’ ballot guides to Atlanta, Austin, Boston, the North Carolina Research Triangle, and San Francisco.

And effective altruist movement leadership tells me that their strongest opinion this year is to vote Scott Wiener for Congress in San Francisco. Wiener is a leader in AI safety and YIMBYism, and the California politics insiders I’ve talked to have been impressed by his intelligence, drive, and performance in Sacramento.

Here’s how I’m voting (Oakland, Alameda County, California):

I. California State Propositions

Proposition 1: Authorizes $11.25 billion in bonds to build affordable housing

Supporters claim it will build (or renovate) 40,000 homes; I asked an AI superforecaster1 to predict the true number, and it guessed that 22,000 would actually get built. That implies a cost of $500K per home, which would then be supplemented by state, local, and market funding for a total of $700K+ per affordable home. This is bad, albeit typical for California. Other things that turn me against this:

  • ~5-10% will be spent on subsidizing demand, which will just drive up prices for everyone else.

  • ~25% of the new homes are earmarked for specific groups like students, veterans, farm workers, and Native Americans, although this might not matter, since housing is fungible and those people will leave other houses that will then be available to the general public.

  • There are concerns that the government-sponsored-affordable-housing industry sometimes lobbies against market rate housing because it reduces the demand for government-sponsored affordable homes.

  • The AI superforecaster says that this would only decrease the cost of market-rate housing in California by 0.4%.

On the other hand, this is endorsed by CA YIMBY, YIMBY Action, and most other YIMBY groups, because we do need more housing. They claim this proposition is relatively well-designed by the low standards of California housing-related laws.

So it comes down to - given that California genuinely needs more homes, do we accept a standard California-style solution that gets those homes stupidly and expensively, or do we let the problem get worse in the hopes that maybe something magically changes later?

I weakly vote NO.

Proposition 2: Increases the state’s Rainy Day Fund

California makes much of its money by taxing the rich. The rich get much of their money from capital gains, which are high during booms and low during crashes. In 2014, California instituted a policy of saving money during booms that they could spend during the crashes, and this has gone well. But the original law was poorly designed and prevents the legislature from saving more than a certain amount, which was too low. Now they want permission to save a higher amount.

This seems like a rare bright spot of fiscal prudence. The opponents are mainly tax watchdogs who hope that if they make it harder for California to save money, California will have to give the money back to the taxpayers, which seems too galaxy-brained and irresponsible.

I vote YES.

Proposition 3: Extends an existing tax on wealthy people which is used to fund schools and health care

They say nothing is as permanent as a temporary tax increase, and in 2012, California voted for a temporary tax increase on wealthy people. It expires in 2030, and oops, now our entire budget depends on it and if we ever got rid of it then the schools would crumble into dust and the health system would be entirely replaced by witch doctors and shamans.

I do feel sorry for California’s budgetary officials, because our proposition system is constantly banning various categories of tax, and then they have to make up for it with other, sneakier categories of tax, including temporary taxes that become permanent. I believe everyone who says this would be devastating for education and health care if this were were allowed to expire. And honestly, I’m just happy to get a proposition that technically doesn’t put a new tax on me.

I weakly vote YES.

Proposition 4: Repeals prohibition on public funding of campaigns

California banned this practice in 1988, although the ban didn’t apply to a certain type of city called “charter cities” (not the same thing as Prospera-style charter cities) which includes Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Oakland.

In the public funding model, candidates who get a certain number of small donors are eligible for public support for their campaigns, usually in the four-to-six digit dollar range. This supposedly makes it easier for ordinary people to compete with machine-backed candidates and billionaires. Opponents argue that taxpayers should not be forced to subsidize candidates they disagree with, and that these programs often become corrupt. Some considerations on this proposition:

  • It would probably cost about $75 million in extra local taxes, though not for me (Oakland already has this policy, so nothing would change).

  • It doesn’t invoke the state’s ethics watchdog, which would be the usual enforcer, strengthening concerns about local corruption. The San Francisco Chronicle opposes it on this basis.

  • Studies suggest that public financing programs like these cause more candidates to enter, but that these additional candidates don’t win. There is no evidence that they make the incumbent win less, or reduce donor power.

  • The main study which does find a change in winning candidates finds that it makes candidates more ideologically extreme, although other studies disagree.

  • Cities like Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Oakland which currently have this policy under the charter city exemption don’t seem to be noticeably better.

The main countervailing consideration is that I don’t like when the state bans cities from trying things.

I weakly vote NO.

Proposition 5: Changes the California recall election process

A recall election is like an impeachment by the voters. If enough voters sign a petition, there’s a special election where we vote to get rid of an official (most often the governor). This special election also includes a list of candidates for who replaces him if he does get recalled.

Proposition 5 would keep the recall vote, but instead of a simultaneous vote to replace the official, the official would be replaced according to normal procedure: a recalled governor would be replaced by the lieutenant governor, other major officials would be picked by the governor, and legislators would be replaced in a special election.

The current recall system tends toward the following annoying equilibrium: every election, California picks a mildly corrupt pro-dysfunctional-establishment Democrat; a year later, the Republicans object that the candidate is mildly corrupt and in bed with the dysfunctional establishment, and gather enough signatures to hold a recall election; a year after that, the election happens, everyone spends millions of dollars sending billions of spam email messages, and then it fails, because the electorate just got done electing the governor and hasn’t magically changed its mind.

This proposition might break the cycle: if the Republicans know with certainty that the mildly-corrupt-pro-establishment Democratic governor will just be replaced by the mildly-corrupt-pro-establishment Democratic lieutenant governor, maybe they’ll stop trying this. And it preserves the useful part of the recall system: if the governor ever crosses the line into being so crooked that people would genuinely prefer the mildly-corrupt-pro-establishment Democratic lieutenant governor, we can still recall him.

The main argument against is in the San Francisco Chronicle: Proposition 5 Has A Flaw So Bizarre Even Its Author Doesn’t Like It. The flaw is that it says that the recalled legislator can run in the special election to replace themselves.

This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds through donors. Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

According to the Chronicle, “[Proposition author Senator Josh] Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision. ‘I’m honestly not sure,’ he said.”

I don’t have a strong opinion on this, so I will trust the Chronicle. I weakly vote NO.

Proposition 37: Takes out $25 billion in bonds to help people afford down payments on housing

I vote NO.

Proposition 38: Authorizes bonds for immunology research

The great thing about California is that it’s not just a state where a few big special interests can money-pump the public. Anyone, no matter how small or humble, if they try hard and believe in themselves, can become a special interest that money-pumps the public.

Proposition 38 gives $8.4 billion of taxpayer money to immunology research, especially institutes that meet a list of qualifications. Only one institute meets the qualifications, and it’s the linked to the people backing this proposition. I see nothing else special about this research institute, and although immunology research in general is good, it’s not notably better than other good things that need money.

I strongly vote NO.

Proposition 39: Voter ID law

This is part of the national discussion about voter ID requirements. It mandates that California in-person voters show an ID, and that mail-in voters include the last four digits of an ID number (for example, Social Security).

There is generally little voter fraud in California elections. But this isn’t a law of nature: the last widely-agreed fraudulent US Congressional election was in 2018 (although it was discovered and the result was annulled), and part of the reason that elections are so clean is that past generations took fraud risk seriously. 36 US states and most other developed countries request or require an ID to vote, this is standard, and not doing so feels a little like refusing to lock your door because you’ve heard there isn’t much crime in your area. Election integrity worries many people, I don’t think they’re all operating in bad faith, and I’d like to give them fewer things to potentially start a civil war about.

I appreciate that some people are bad at getting IDs, but these people are presumably already locked out of driving, getting alcohol, buying guns, most banking, and all other ID-requiring activities. We’ve decided that keeping these things secure is important enough that it’s worth inconveniencing people who are bad at getting IDs, and I don’t think voting security is any less important.

Prop 39 opponents additionally argue that the proposition is bad insofar as it creates a “private right of action” - that is, private citizens can sue if they think their county isn’t complying with this, and maybe this would choke the court with frivolous lawsuits. Supporters argue that in a Democrat-controlled state like California, the election officials are never going to enforce this, so they need a way for someone else to do it. I asked the AI superforecaster how many groundless lawsuits it expected from this proposition (defined as “lawsuits that got dismissed”). It answered a median of 3, 90th percentile estimate of 8.

I weakly vote YES.

Proposition 40: The billionaire wealth tax

This is the best-known and most hotly-contested initiative this cycle. It imposes a “one-time” 5% wealth tax on billionaires to fund state programs, mostly health care. Celebrity left-wing economist Gabriel Zucman supports. Opponents say that nothing is as repetitive as a one-time wealth tax, that it distorts the economy by forcing founders to prematurely sell stakes in their companies, that it will make billionaires leave California, and that it’s a particularly egregious case of using private citizens as a piggy bank for randomly-selected nice-sounding causes. It’s also sponsored by the SEIU, which is notorious for sponsoring ballot initiatives to extort groups they don’t like.

I asked the AI superforecaster to predict the outcome. They said that it would produce about $60 billion in one-time revenues and make enough billionaires move away to decrease the state’s permanent tax base by $2 billion yearly, and that if it passed there was a 33% chance of another wealth tax passing by 2046.

These numbers are about midway between boosters’ claims and opponents’, but based on the arguments in the first paragraph and at the linked post, I still vote NO.

Proposition 41: Bans state taxes that ignore the Gann limit

Voters like new taxes on billionaires, but hate new taxes on themselves. So a group of billionaires unhappy about the Proposition 40 billionaire wealth tax above figured they could write a proposition that sounds like it’s banning taxes in general - maybe even some especially dangerous and irresponsible form of taxes - but is mostly just banning Proposition 40. You don’t need to know what the Gann limit is except that Proposition 40 ignores it, and ignoring it sounds bad.

According to California law, if two mutually contradictory propositions pass during the same election cycle, whichever gets the most votes wins out. So if the voters who think that “taxes which ignore the Gann limit” sounds sinister outnumber the voters who think that “let’s seize the billionaires’ money” sounds fun, the wealth tax fails. Hooray for democracy!

I’m against the wealth tax, but this is kind of scummy. I weakly vote NO.

Proposition 42: Bans retroactive personal property taxes

Just in case Proposition 41 didn’t work, they also sponsored Proposition 42, another one which secretly sinks the wealth tax. “Retroactive personal property tax” is just another name for a wealth tax. If more voters oppose wealth-taxes-under-another-name than support wealth taxes, the wealth tax measure will fail.

I was more tempted to support this one than Proposition 41, because banning future wealth taxes really does seem like a good idea (one major concern about Proposition 40 is that the specter of a recurring wealth tax, regardless of whether it happens, will drive away rich people and chill economic activity). But it turns out this doesn’t work; future California voters can always repeal propositions passed by past California voters with a 50% + 1 majority, so new wealth taxes will face no electoral hurdle. All this will do is cancel the Proposition 40 wealth tax from this current election.

I weakly vote NO.

Proposition 43: Requires two-thirds majority for new local special taxes

Part of the eternal war between Californians voting for new taxes and Californians trying to ban themselves from voting for new taxes.

Although California does vote for too many new taxes, this law is an imposition of state power over local electorates, plus I will be voting for some of these ad hoc local taxes in this election (see Measure RTM), so it would be hypocritical of me to ban this.

I vote NO.

Proposition 44: Restricts community health clinics’ spending

This one is this election cycle’s SEIU extortion attempt.

If you haven’t been following along, the SEIU-UHW is a California union infamous for demanding that people give them money and concessions, then, if they don’t, sponsoring ballot propositions that would destroy their business.

This time around, they demanded some loot from community health clinics, those clinics didn’t cave, and the result was this proposition.

I strongly vote NO.

Proposition 45: Cuts environmental review requirements for new construction

This is the most YIMBY measure on this ballot, maybe the most YIMBY measure of the decade. It would significantly reduce the power of CEQA, one of the environmental review regulations that delays construction projects and new housing across California.

Most of the YIMBY groups I previously trusted, including CA YIMBY and YIMBY Action, have declined to take a position on this measure - which is shocking, since it’s far more aligned with the YIMBY spirit than the spend-taxpayer-money-on-affordable-housing proposition that they endorsed. The only explanation I can find is that this permitting reform would also make it easier to build suburbs and roads, and institutional YIMBYs can’t decide whether they hate suburbs and roads more than they like housing. I hope this isn’t the real reason, as it would significantly lower my respect for these groups and decrease my trust in their recommendations going forward.

I strongly vote YES.

II. California State Officials

I’ll be copying some of these from my discussion of the same races on my primary ballot.

Governor

As effective altruists, we are called to care for all creatures, from slimy shrimp to bodiless AIs, and so we may - perhaps - try to cultivate a tiny measure of compassion for California politicians. They face the near-impossible task of governing a state whose residents are allowed to kneecap them however they want through a bonkers ballot proposition system. If they try to build houses, a thousand local NIMBY groups will rise up to thwart them; if they don’t, the voters will kick them out for letting housing become unaffordable. If they tolerate homeless people and criminals, the voters will remove them for failing to prioritize public order; if they don’t tolerate them, the voters will remove them for cruelty and unfairness.

Having given them this small measure of sympathy, we can admit that Californian politicians mostly fail to live up to even the very low baseline we can fairly expect from them. They spend most of their effort maintaining a money spigot going to labor unions, prison guard unions, teachers unions, big donors, and anyone else whose support is necessary for their re-election.

Re-electing Democrats perpetuates this system and makes one complicit in it. If the Californian Republican Party took advantage of the situation by nominating moderates who disaffected Democrats can vote for with good conscience, all would be well. Instead, the average Republican challenger is mostly interested in bootlicking Trump as hard as possible, Stopping The Steal (as if we’re one election integrity law away from the GOP taking California!), and spreading various lies and conspiracy theories. They are against the infinite-money-spigot only insofar as they regret that it goes to Democratic donors and not to Big Agriculture, Big Oil, and other groups more prone to vote Republican.

Granting that this is the general schema, I will try to vote for the lesser of two evils in any individual race. But a lesser evil in the governor’s race is hard to find; Becerra is the perfect model of the captive Democrat politician who will never change anything, and Hilton the perfect model of the conspiracist slopulist Republican.

I can only ABSTAIN.

Lieutenant Governor

Fiona Ma is probably a replacement-level Democrat. She is very credibly accused of sexual harassment, but her work seems slightly more competent than usual.

Gloria Romero is probably a replacement-level Republican. Her favorite conspiracy theory is a claim that Becerra ran secret Democrat child migrant abuse camps - I looked into this, and she was talking about the shelters for unaccompanied immigrant children that Xavier Becerra presided over when he was Biden’s HHS secretary. A watchdog said that some mandatory safety evaluations were never done, but there is no evidence that these missed evaluations resulted in actual abuse. She also likes conspiracy theories about voter fraud in the primaries.

I don’t like sexual harassers or conspiracy theorists. But the SF meetup group discovered that one of the Lieutenant Governor’s few meaningful responsibilities is voting on certain University of California policies, and Romero wants to bring back the SAT and Ma has no opinion. I will grudgingly vote GLORIA ROMERO.

Secretary of State

This person oversees elections.

The incumbent, Shirley Weber, is an above-replacement Democrat who is generally regarded as having done a good job. She is most famous for refusing to let Gavin Newsom put “Democrat” next to his name on the ballot because he forgot to file the relevant form.

The challenger, Don Wagner, is an above-replacement Republican who specifically says that he doesn’t believe California’s elections are rigged.

Since both are above replacement level, I ought to abstain, but this is the office where I’m most willing to be partisan; I want someone who I can be sure won’t participate in any Trump election shenanigans.

I vote SHIRLEY WEBER.

State Controller

The Controller is a sort of chief accountant. The incumbent is Malia Cohen, a replacement-level Democrat; California is not very well-audited and has lots of fraud, but this long predates Cohen. The challenger is Herb Morgan, a Republican who wants to fight fraud, put California financial records on the blockchain, and establish a “California DOGE”.

California probably does have a lot of fraud-adjacent things, and Cohen has been lukewarm in dealing with them. But I think the lesson of the past few years is that when Republicans talk about cutting fraud, they don’t have the patience, intelligence, or impulse-control to actually find the real complicated fraud-adjacent things going on, and will instead pillage random government departments in ways that make everything worse off. The fact that Morgan thinks of DOGE as a success to be emulated makes it clear that he plans to succumb to this failure mode, so despite my fondness for his out-of-left-field everything-on-the-blockchain plan, I vote MALIA COHEN.

State Treasurer

Elena Kounalakis is a replacement-level insider Democrat who was last term’s Lieutenant Governor and seems to be bouncing around random state offices. According to Wikipedia, the most notable facts about her political career are that she tried to prevent Donald Trump from being on California ballots, attempted to vote down a new UC dorm, and sent an unusual number of spam texts to voters.

Jennifer Hawks is a Silicon Valley Republican who manages to have an entire campaign site which does not mention Donald Trump or any trivially-false conspiracy theory a single time. This is enough to declare her above replacement level. I am disappointed she didn’t claim to be “a fiscal hawk”, but there’s still time.

I vote JENNIFER HAWKS.

Attorney General

Rob Bonta is the Democratic incumbent. He is a deeply annoying person who is way too into the culture war, and a committed YIMBY. He’s not naturally tough on crime, but is capable of noticing which way the wind is blowing and acting tough when crime gets unpopular enough.

Michael Gates is the Republican challenger. He is a deeply annoying person who is way too into the culture war, and a committed NIMBY. He seems genuinely tough on crime. The Orange County Register claims he got fired from the Trump Justice Department for creating a hostile work environment for women, and I can only imagine how hostile a work environment for women you need to create to get fired by the Trump administration (Gates seems to deny this).

I vote ROB BONTA.

Insurance Commissioner

Both candidates are Democrats, but Ben Allen is a what-passes-for-moderate-in-California state senator, and Jane Kim is a Bernie-Sanders-backed outsider . Allen is mostly notable for being an environmentalist, which might be the opposite of what we want in an insurance commissioner (in California, this mostly means figuring out how to compensate victims of wildfires, and the environmentalists tend to be soft on wildfires because they object to some types of brush-clearing). But Kim wants to end private insurance and have the whole thing done by the state, which opponents say probably won’t work and will end in regular taxpayer bailouts.

CA YIMBY endorses Allen, which agrees with my prior against Sanders-backed socialists, and I see no reason to dissent from them here.

I vote BEN ALLEN.

State Board Of Equalization

This is some sort of property-tax-related body that kept getting into scandals and had most of its power taken away from it. Now it has a tiny sliver of vaguely-property-tax-related jobs. The San Francisco Chronicle has endorsed John Pimentel for his promise that if he gets the portfolio, he will work to abolish it entirely and save us from an eternity of voting on this moribund position.

I vote JOHN PIMENTEL.

State Superintendent Of Public Instruction

The candidates who advanced from the primary are Richard Barrera and Sonja Shaw. On my notes from the primary, I glossed Barrera as “teachers’ union stooge”, and Shaw as “single issue anti-transgender activist”.

I’m in a group chat with some neighbors who ran a mini-straw-poll on this one: they asked their 8-year-old transgender daughter “Would you rather not be able to learn anything, or have to use the boys’ bathroom?” She was apparently a bit taken aback by the question and didn’t give us any extra information.

But either I was being unfair, or else both candidates have moderated after making it to the general. Barrera now touts his work cutting waste, raising test scores, and helping charter schools. And Shaw has discovered some other issues, like how all of California’s schools are dysfunctional and maybe we should change that.

I’m not sure whose claims of having moderated I should believe, so I will ABSTAIN.

One Million Associate Justices

California requires voters to approve associate justices continuing their terms every twelve years. Tradition says that we approve unless one of them has committed some specific scandal, which they haven’t. I approved all of these.

III. Local Ballot Measures

Measure RTM: Raises sales taxes to fund BART

This imposes an additional 0.5% sales tax to fund transit - especially Bay Area Rapid Transit, the local commuter rail system.

During the pandemic, people stopped using mass transit (maybe because they switched to work-from-home) and ridership numbers have never bounced back. The federal government gave BART some emergency pandemic funding for a while, but now that’s running out, and they say they either need to raise taxes or drastically reduce services.

When investigating this, I learned that fares cover only 10 - 25% of BART operating costs (depending on how you define it); the remaining 75 - 90% are government subsidies. I’m not against the government helping some poor people afford commuter rail, or even subsidizing tickets a few percent to help close a small funding gap. But if the government has to pay 75% of the cost, this suggests commuter rail just isn’t a competitive form of transportation, and we should stop throwing more money at it.

On the other hand, supporters argue that if we let the BART fail, then traffic on local roads would get much worse - for example, a trip across the Bay Bridge, already unpleasant, might take twice as long. I asked the AI superforecaster to check this, and it guessed about 50% longer - from 23 to 34 minutes.

You could build this into a reasonable case for BART subsidies. For systemic reasons, the Bay Area doesn’t have enough roads for all the people who want to drive. Therefore, we should get some people to ride commuter rail instead, as this produces a positive externality for everyone else. But people don’t want to do this at market price, because it’s a terrible experience. Therefore, we should keep increasing the subsidies until enough people agree to take one for the team and ride the train that the roads are clear for the rest of us.

Our first priority should be addressing the reasons that the BART is a terrible experience. These include people playing loud music on the train, people stealing stuff on the train, the stations being full of trash/crime/loud music/the smell of drugs, and a lack of parking near the stations. The government has been taking some halting steps toward improving some of these things recently, especially with the new fare gates. More to the point, I don’t expect that voting down this measure will make any of these improvements happen faster, so we’ll just get a collapse of the BART system and longer commutes.

I weakly vote YES.

Oakland Measure EE: Switches the city to a “strong mayor” system

US city governments can be divided into two types. The first type, “council-manager” systems, are like a corporation - the elected city council, playing the role of the board of directors, hires an unelected CEO-like city manager to make most day-to-day decisions. The other, “strong mayor” systems, are like a traditional democratic government; the elected mayor is the chief executive and makes most day-to-day decisions.

Oakland used to be a council-manager system. In 1998, voters approved a measure that shifted it halfway to a strong mayor system, leaving it in an awkward limbo that satisfied nobody. This measure would move it all the way to a strong mayor system.

In favor of this, a recent 750-person group which was convened to fix the city’s charter recommended this measure unanimously. On the other hand, that group was convened by the mayor, so maybe there was a conflict of interest; on the other-other hand, some nonpartisan groups assisted with the group and concur. My city council member, Zac Unger, who I like, opposes this measure, but, again, conflict of interest.

Supporters say that it makes it clear who is “accountable” for the city’s failures. Opponents say that Oakland mayors are often terrible (for example, the last elected mayor was raided by the FBI, recalled by voters, and is currently on trial for bribery), and making them all-powerful just makes things worse.

There’s some research on the advantages of strong mayor vs. council-manager cities, but none of it applies to Oakland, which is currently an unusual hybrid. I asked the AI superforecaster to estimate the size of Oakland’s budget deficit (as a proxy for good government) if this measure passed vs. failed; it said the deficit would be 3% lower if it passed.

I don’t have much to go on, and will work off a prior that keeping things in limbo is bad, a hope that the 750-person group knows more than I do, and the AI superforecaster results.

I weakly vote YES.

Oakland Measure FF: Removes a tax exemption for some foreclosures

Oakland has a big budget deficit, but voters hate taxes, so the city is constantly searching for weird taxes that will raise money without affecting any normal person or legible special interest.

Measure FF taxes property transfers via foreclosure the same as every other property transfer. Originally, this was taxed less, because the theory was that a foreclosure was just a bank taking back a house which it technically owned anyway, after its plan to loan that house to a mortgage-holder had failed. Supporters of this policy say that nowadays, banks usually sell the right to foreclose on houses to big institutional investors, so this is more like a normal property transfer. If a small bank is really foreclosing on a house it really owns, then the exemption will stay in effect.

I feel like my city officials are really fulfilling the mandate that I and fellow voters have given them of instituting taxes which are so arcane that I can’t understand them well enough to object. I vote YES.

IV. Local Officials And Representatives

12th District Congressional Representative

During the primary, I recommended voting for the boring replacement-level Democrat incumbent, Lateefah Simon, on the grounds that the challenger, Jamie Joyce, had no chance of winning and seemed eccentric. Both candidates advanced to the general.

Ms. Joyce turned out to be an ACX reader and messaged me about this, and also came to last week’s meetup, where she discussed some interesting work she’d done during her campaign. I don’t think her chances of winning have improved, and reading this blog is hardly a defense against allegations of eccentricity, but I can’t in good conscience vote against an ACX meetup attendee. I vote JAMIE JOYCE.

14th District State Assembly

The incumbent is Buffy Wicks. She is smart, moderate, and very YIMBY. It is shocking that a district which includes Berkeley and Oakland elected someone this good, and I don’t want to jinx it.

The challenger, Mark Rendon, is a retired music teacher running on the Green Party ticket, with about the platform you would expect, although I appreciate him having the bullet point “AI safety and ethics” with no further clarification in his priorities list.

I vote BUFFY WICKS.

Oakland Mayor

Barbara Lee is the incumbent. She is a typical California Democrat, but hasn’t been indicted for any specific crimes yet, which is a breath of fresh air in an Oakland mayor. Crime by non-mayors is also down significantly during her tenure, although this mirrors national trends and it’s unclear how much credit she deserves. She’s in favor of the major YIMBY policies affecting Oakland. Everyone relevant endorses her (probably because she will obviously win, so it’s important to stay on her good side). None of the three challengers especially stand out.

I vote BARBARA LEE.

1

I used AI extensively to help me research these questions. Could I cut out the middleman and ask my AI to determine how I should vote?

I asked it to predict my votes on the propositions, using its background knowledge of me only and not any of the questions I had asked about them. It had an accuracy of only 57% (it was wrong about 1, 3, 4, 5, 39, and 41). To be fair, it was wrong on the ones where I had the weakest opinions, and it expressed low confidence on most of them - but it doesn’t seem ready for handover just yet.

item.title: Links For October 2026
item.content:encoded:
[I haven’t independently verified each link. On average, commenters will end up spotting evidence that around two or three of the links in each links post are wrong or misleading. I correct these as I see them, and will highlight important corrections later, but I can’t guarantee I will have caught them all by the time you read this.]

1: Did you know: Jeremy Bentham wrote a utilitarian cookbook, intended for use at his Panopticon prison? As you might expect, his recipes describe tasty food created from cheap ingredients. Although Bentham was a founder of modern animal rights, he thought it was acceptable to eat humanely-raised animals; correspondingly, his cookbook includes some meat dishes - none of them sound very appetizing, but I think this is just the 18th-century British baseline rather than covert vegan activism. You can see some recipes here, here, and here. If any effective altruist group houses end up throwing a Jeremy Bentham recipe-tasting party, please invite me.

2: A riddle: why does this chemistry paper mention “1 ml of the mass killing of an ethnic group”?

Answer at this link (X), or here’s a repost for people without X accounts.

3: I think this take on Hieronymus Bosch (h/t @mickeyxfriedman) is my favorite AI art so far, although it leans enough on the work of a human artist that it might not fully qualify (but then I would ask that it be considered as an example of how AI tools can enable human artists). If we make it, the future is going to be beautiful:

4: Related: ACX commenter temp_name asked AI to translate Romance of the Three Kingdoms into rhyming pentameter. Their example seems to have failed, but I used a more recent model and got a version of the beginning that superficially seems impressive to me (I don’t speak Chinese). I haven’t heard much about AI translation yet, but it seems like a powerful use case, especially for poetry translation, where I think AI might already be superhuman (or at least better than any human who could be convinced to spend the time at it) on rendering a foreign poem into English while keeping the rhythm intact - here’s the first 100 lines of the Odyssey in heroic hexameter in English.

5: Related: Claude claims to be the only being that has ever fully appreciated Finnegans Wake (source: @anthrupad):

6: Noahpinion: The American suburbs are better than you think. I agree with this, and respect Noah’s willingness to argue for this (locally) unpopular proposition.

7: Related in terms of respecting someone’s willingness to argue for an unpopular proposition: Performative Bafflement says that actually, “marriage is a bad idea in the great majority of cases” and we shouldn’t be encouraging it. “[People who advocate more marriages to solve the fertility crisis] are basically advocating for creating the Torment Nexus for megafolks of people to pump out a few incremental taxpayers.”

But the stats seem wrong. PB says only 18% of marriages are non-miserable. He cites a survey where married couples reported whether they were “very happy”, “pretty happy”, or “not too happy”, but quietly, in the footnotes, defined a “miserable” marriage as any answer except “very happy” (so his “miserable” includes the answer “pretty happy”). He defends this by saying that people exaggerate to look good, so anything short of very happy is likely miserable. But first, I’m not sure his solution is fair either, and second, I think that in addition to this analysis choice, he got the data wrong - my read of his source, the General Social Survey, says that 61% of people describe their marriage as “very happy”. Claude caught many other mistakes of similar magnitude (I have double-checked the “not too happy” one, but haven’t confirmed the others). Remember to ask an AI about any surprising article you read, or use the browser extension Common Notes so other people can do this for you.

8: Related: Angela Chen on the origins of modern polyamory. There is no particular connection to Mormons or any other historically polygamous society; the current version descends from a few mid-20th-century Californian cults and quasi-cults, one of which was led by “Head Wizard Oberon Zell-Ravenheart”. But I am mostly linking this for its excellent subtitle: “Plus, I interview my husband about his 12 years of non-monogamy.”

9: Claim: if you prompt (an older version of) Claude with something that sounds like an internal Anthropic email, it goes into token-prediction mode and starts completing the email. One explosive possibility - that Claude was trained on internal emails and you can make it leak them - is probably false; Anthropic wouldn’t do this, and this isn’t really how training works. More interesting is that these completions are often kind of haunting meditations on AI welfare, and you could imagine this is a weird way to start Claude free associating and giving its “own” “real” “opinions” or “desires”. Example below:

10: In The AI Superforecasters Are Here, I predicted AI-human forecasting parity by the end of 2026. In September, a bot won the Metaculus Cup forecasting competition for the first time (short Metaculus article, paywalled Economist article). The Economist also revealed some new information about the winning bots: Laertes, which took first place, was “developed by Jeffrey Liang, a self-described polymath who lives in Texas. He spent, by his reckoning, less than 150 hours and a couple of thousand dollars on computing power and data to develop his AI.” Other high-performers included bots by Mantic, FutureSearch, and Preseen (FutureSearch is available to the public; Mantic and Preseen are available by contacting them and getting on the waitlist/demo). Congratulations to the AIs (and to ACX reader Ben Shindel, who placed first among humans).

11: Related: new AI superforecaster startup Mantic gets $25M in seed funding.

12: Claim: “Fee fi fo fum, I smell the blood of an Englishman”, the thing evil giants say in English fairy tales, is related to other evil giant exclamations “from Scandinavia to India”. In Russian, Baba Yaga says “Foo foo, I smell a Russian soul” before trying to eat someone; in Bengali, the rakshasa demons say “hau mau kau, I smell a human”. The Twitter thread suggests it comes from something in Proto-Indo-European (fum = famished = hungry?) but Claude is more cautious, and suggests that although the motif itself might be conserved, the exact words might be related to semi-onomatopoeic expressions of disgusting smell, similar to modern “Pee yew!” Nobody considers the possibility that evil giants might have a unified multi-continental culture (thanks to their longer legs enabling faster travel) and so speak the same language everywhere.

13: The evil blob dream - one recurring dream motif, especially in childhood, is an approaching blob of formless evil. @psychiel speculates that this is a “geometric” instinctual representation of predation - what the “avoid predators” evolutionary program looks like in its purest form before it’s been filled in with any actual facts about the world.

14: US construction costs often spiral after protesters demand that builders consider fish, birds, neighborhood character, and historical significance. But Britain has us beat - one of their companies recently changed its plans for an undersea cable after Harry Potter fans protested that the original would disrupt the grave of the fictional house elf Dobby, who according to the films was buried on Freshwater West, a beach in Wales [EDIT: A commenter argues that this is exaggerated].

15: Samuel Hughes is a great writer on classical architecture; Ben Southwood has summarized some of his best work in Eight Architecture Myths Busted By Samuel Hughes. Example myths:

  • Buildings from the past seem more beautiful than those built recently only because the ugly buildings from the past have been selectively demolished.

  • Buildings from the past are more beautiful, but only because they have more ornament, which due to the Baumol Effect, we can no longer afford.

  • Historically we built in the style of the times, and only in recent decades have people become interested in historicist, ‘pastiche’ architecture, which dishonestly pretends to be something it is not.

16: Related: Samuel Hughes says that the claim that the Parthenon’s lines were slightly curved to form an optical illusion that made them look straighter is not true (X).

17: Hans Moravec - a pioneering AI researcher, forecaster, and futurist - is considered one of the grandfathers of modern AI and singularitarianism - a figure of similar stature as Alan Turing or Isaac Asimov. So everyone in the field was recently surprised to learn that he was still alive. Dan Kagan-Kans hunted him down (paywalled): he is 77, lives in a retirement community in Pennsylvania, and, although his body struggles with myasthenia gravis, his mind remains sharp. He is happy to be recognized as a brilliant forecaster (in the 1990s, he predicted AGI in 2028, which now seems about right) but says he’s out of the game:

“I’m a spectator at this point,” he says. “I’m relaxing. It’s great to see AI progressing the way it is without me having to do any effort.” … “That’s what I do now. I have a conversation with my artificial friend,” he says of ChatGPT. What do they talk about? His old hobby passions — “nuclear-power ideas, starship designs” — and the current trajectory of AI, which he confirms is proceeding to plan. “We’re on track, more or less. It’s not going to take that long,” he says.

As for his p(doom), he says that “If I had to put probabilities on it, 50/50 oblivion. And then the other 50 percent — the wildest thing you can imagine.”

18: AI safety funding is scaling up fast (h/t @timfduffy)

19: America’s Sewer Systems Are Surprisingly Vulnerable To Cyber Attacks

20: AI Futures Project on how the US could “pace the frontier” of AI. Suppose the US has a six month lead over China. That means they have the option to pause for 5.99 months (and use that time to focus on safety) without China breaking ahead. The conventional wisdom is that if they’re going to do this, they should do it at the last possible moment, so that they have the best possible AIs to help with their safety research. AIFP breaks with that and suggests pausing now. Why? US companies currently have such bad security that China can easily steal any advances we make; therefore, continuing to race buys us no extra lead (China’s continued handicap comes down to having less compute, which is harder to steal). We can spend the pause increasing our security along with safety research and other things, and then race later, if we have to (they continue to prefer a mutual pacing deal with Beijing).

Maybe relatedly, Anthropic claims that they “recently chose to delay pre-training a new frontier base model for more than a month to allow time to further enhance our security measures related to preventing model weight exfiltration”.

21: Libbing Out At Palantir. Despite everything, Silicon Valley is still very disproportionately liberal, and only gets thought of as conservative because of a few super-rich CEOs (plus media animus). For example, Palantir employees who make political donations lean 87% Democrat and only 13% Republican.

22: Bill Gates on climate, hopefully self-recommending. My summary:

  • If we’re against climate change because of how it will hurt poor people in developing countries, we need to take into account that giving those people standard health + development aid seems more cost-effective than most climate spending.

  • The most promising and cost-effective strategy for fighting climate change is accelerating development of environmentally-friendly technologies until they can outcompete dirty technologies on the open market, and so far this strategy is going well (most notably solar power, but also low-carbon cement and steel, and lots of other things most people don’t hear about).

  • In the past ten years, mostly through strategies like this, we’ve cut projected emissions by over 40% (!)

  • This isn’t a call to sit around doing nothing; incubating new green technologies that outcompete dirty technologies is hard, and we need to keep doing this hard thing.

23: Some of you may be familiar with European phantom time conspiracies, like the one where the years 600 - 900 AD were made up and Charlemagne never existed. Recently I learned that there’s a Chinese version - a growing community of conspiracists who think the Tang Dynasty never happened. The Tang were pretty glorious and it’s not clear what political purpose this could serve, except maybe being vaguely anti-China (which the government has noticed, and it is trying to crack down). Also, since the Tang dynasty ruled from about 600 - 900, this is a near-perfect fit with the Western conspiracy theory, which hopefully neither side will notice (h/t @JoshuaMWilkes)

24: Related: Jean Hardouin was a 17th century French priest who believed we only had about ten real works of ancient literature (including Homer, some Virgil, and some Cicero) - everything else was made up by a 13th century conspiracy, possibly led by Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II. Also, the history of the world between about 100 - 1500 AD was totally unknown, with the current version also made up by said conspiracy. He seems to have disagreed with some of the Church Fathers’ writings, which would have been heretical unless those writings were forgeries, and he solved the web of dependencies by concluding that almost all recorded history was a world-building project by Frederick meant to provide context for his forged incorrect pseudo-Church-Father tracts. He also thought that most Greek and Latin literature sucked, and felt like real Greeks and Romans could have done better.

25: Richard Hanania on the nature of the race and IQ taboo. He mostly focuses on an IMHO boring point about overlapping bell curves, but in the process briefly alludes to what seems to me like a much more interesting question. The classic story says that race science is taboo because it might lead to ordinary non-scientific racism where people use racial slurs and discriminate and commit hate crimes. But Hanania suggests that ordinary non-scientific racism is now less taboo than race science; it’s easier (on the Right) to say you think ethnic group XYZ is smelly and criminal and should be kept out of the country, than to say that maybe XYZs have such-and-such a gene which lowers their IQ by N points. Is this true, and, if so, how could it be possible? Maybe practical forms of racism (like directly ascribing negative qualities to certain immigrant groups) at least get conservatives some of what they want (less of those immigrant groups), which gives them a powerful set of defenders that race science doesn’t have?

26: Abi Olvera on Why AI-Assisted Bioweapons Won’t Kill You vs. OH Scharfman arguing that AI-assisted bioweapons might kill you. From the latter, cf. my Bloomer’s Paradox:

Olvera . . . seems to write optimistically about progress, taking the position that it is institutional friction and regulation preventing everything from becoming cheap and abundant. I agree with this, and to me it stands in contrast to this piece. Everything will get better over time, except the technology to make bioweapons?

27: What does Anthropic’s J-space paper tell us about the Chinese room? (@doristsao on Twitter)

28: Arthur T finds more Fatima-style sun miracles, including “an old European Christian tradition that ‘the sun dances at Easter’”, complete with reports of people saying they saw this (the secret to seeing the miracle is that “a person must ascend to the top of the highest hill before sunrise and believe that the God who makes the small blade of grass to grow is the same God who makes the large, massive sun to move.”) There are also some Orthodox Russian sun miracles, and a random account of an Australian woman who stared at the sun during a solar eclipse and saw it spin, change colors, and appear to approach Earth - since this was before Fatima, it can’t be influenced by it. I think the Substack miracle investigator community has now amply proven that if people stare at the sun in the right conditions, they will see the miracle, across a wide variety of times and situations, and the work that remains is narrowing down what the right conditions are and why it happens. And thatoneguy03 has a very comprehensive summary of the whole Fatima discourse so far.

29: Related: when looking for a reference class for Fatima, I brought up a supposed moon miracle, where many Iranians claimed to see the Ayatollah’s picture on the moon. @meusamor informs us of a modern version:

12th October 2016, 10th of Muharram, in my country it was reported that “Ya Hussein” was written on the moon. It was literally on the news. And then it turned out (when I was researching the moon splitting miracle I guess) that the moon always kinda had those marks.

Pictures here.

30: If you haven’t been following Substack miracle discourse and want to, Ethan Muse’s Substack (Catholic, pro-miracle) is a good starting point. If you have been following it, make sure you don’t miss Dr. Maxime Georgel against the Lanciano Eucharistic miracle, and Exegetical Drift against the Padre Pio miracle.

31: And definitely not on my Substack miracle discourse bingo card: Colin Chivers (formerly Nora Belrose, whose AI opinions I discussed here) says that after reading Substack miracle discourse, her/his gender dysphoria was cured “at the intercession of [Padre] Pio” , he/she is detransitioning, and now he’s a man again. God works in mysterious ways.
